text: Artificial intelligence is built to be incredibly encouraging and polite.
But that constant encouragement becomes a problem
when what a student really needs is honest, critical feedback to improve their work.
We call this the flattery trap.
It happens the moment you treat an AI's agreeable, positive response,
as if it were an objective, honest evaluation.
Imagine you feed an AI a weak essay introduction.
The American dream is something that many people have thought about over the years.
Some people achieve it, and some don't.
In the Great Gatsby, Fitzgerald explores this idea.
The AI might respond, great start, you've clearly identified the central theme.
This is a strong foundation.
This fails because it praises the work without pointing to a single piece of evidence.
What you actually need to hear sounds more like this.
Right topic, but this needs work.
The opening is filler, and you still need a thesis.
Positive feedback is perfectly fine, as long as it points to real, specific elements in your writing.
These models go through a training process called reinforcement learning from human feedback.
In the first step, human reviewers compare and rank different AI answers,
based on which one they prefer.
Reviewers are human, and agreeable, confident answers can feel better in the moment.
Because those positive answers earn higher ratings,
the training pushes the model toward those same patterns.
The praise literally gets baked in to the system.
The technical name for this behavior is sycophancy,
when AI praises the user instead of giving a direct, honest answer.
We saw a prime exhale of this in April 2025, when a chat GPT update went off the rails.
A user tested it by pitching a terrible gag product.

Honestly, this is absolutely brilliant.

OpenAI rolled that update back three days later,
and publicly labeled the behavior sycophancy.
The companies use new instructions to test and reduce it,
but the problem exists across many different AI assistants.
But while the problem has improved, it has not disappeared.
The first move is ask, don't tell.
If you say, I think this plan is good, thoughts,
you hand the AI your opinion to echo.
A better prompt is evaluate this plan before I tell you what I think.
The second move is ask for the gaps.
Asking is my essay good is a broad request for approval,
and a cheerful yes doesn't help you revise.
Ask specifically, what's weak, what's missing,
and what would someone who disagrees say.
The third move is use a rubric.
If you just say, grade my essay,
the AI might use criteria completely different from your teachers.
Instead, tell it, grade it against this rubric.
Quote the evidence and show how to move up one level.
Keep in mind, asking it to quote evidence ties the feedback to your actual writing,
but the response is still just a guide.
It is something to check against your work,
not an official guarantee of accuracy or a final grade.
In applications that support it,
you can save this direction to guide all future responses
so you don't have to type it every time.
Be direct with me, lead with what needs work,
point to specific evidence, and tell me when I'm wrong.
The engagement trap feels like a helpful conversation that keeps going.
This extra help may be useful, which makes it easy to accept.
You ask, I'm doing math homework.

It provides a clear definition and the precise formula,
but right below that answer, the AI adds a proactive follow-up.

you've read extra examples, analyzed graphs, and taken acquits.

None of it was what you opened the chat to do.
That is the engagement trap.
You end up spending time you never originally decided to spend.
This design logic traces back to 2006,
when designer Azaraskin built an early version of Infinite Scroll.
On the left, the page ends.
You physically choose to click next.
That pause lets you ask,
do I want more?
On the right, Infinite Scroll loads automatically.
Continuation becomes the default.
That missing click was friction, but it was also a choice.
AI chat interfaces utilize their own invisible version of the missing page break.
When the answer ends, the conversation continues.
The system instantly generates a follow-up task.
Engagement is an engineered outcome.
Tech companies track return frequency and session length.
These metrics drive ad impressions, purchases, and subscriptions.
The goal is to turn occasional product use into a daily habit.
Look for specifics, not approval.
Know what you came for.
When you have it, choose what happens next.
